questions.q: What does 'blameless' actually mean in a blameless postmortem?
options: No one is ever held accountable for anything, under any circumstances
The document assumes people acted reasonably given what they knew at the time, and focuses on fixing the system rather than the person
The postmortem is anonymous and doesn't name any systems or services
Only managers are allowed to write postmortems
questions.explain: Blameless means the analysis assumes good faith and reasonable judgment under the circumstances, and directs fixes at the system — not that systemic accountability disappears.

questions.q: Why does a postmortem need an 'Impact' section quantified with real numbers rather than a general description?
options: Because vague impact descriptions are against company policy
Because a quantified impact (sessions affected, carts abandoned, duration) makes the severity and cost of the incident concrete instead of impressionistic
Because quantified numbers are required for legal reasons in every case
Because it replaces the need for a timeline section
questions.explain: A specific, quantified impact statement ('p99 latency exceeded 2s for 34 minutes, affecting ~4,100 sessions') gives a concrete sense of severity that 'checkout was slow' cannot.

questions.q: In the Northbridge example, why is 'no alert existed on connection pool saturation' classified as a contributing factor rather than the root cause?
options: Because contributing factors are always more important than root causes
Because it made the incident harder to catch early, but the underlying reason the pool failed was that it had never been load-tested for flash-sale volume
Because alerts are never considered relevant to root cause analysis
Because the on-call engineer configured alerts incorrectly on purpose
questions.explain: The root cause is the technical reason the failure happened (an under-sized, untested pool). The missing saturation alert didn't cause the failure — it made it take longer to detect and diagnose, which is what makes it a contributing factor.

questions.q: Which of these is a well-formed action item from a postmortem?
options: "Improve monitoring for connection pools."
"Add a saturation-based alert on inventory-db pool wait-queue depth. Owner: Priya Shah. Due: before next scheduled flash sale."
"Someone should probably look into this eventually."
"Avoid flash sales in the future."
questions.explain: A real action item needs a specific task, a named owner, and a due date. Without those, it's a wish rather than tracked, committed work.

questions.q: What problem does skipping owners and due dates on action items create?
options: None — action items are informational only
The postmortem's recommendations are unlikely to actually get done, since nothing tracks who is responsible or by when
It makes the timeline section inaccurate
It automatically triggers an escalation
questions.explain: Without an owner and a due date, an action item has no mechanism forcing it to completion — the postmortem's analysis doesn't translate into real system improvement.
